en: The Brahmāyu Sūtra, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Sūrpāraka together with five hundred śramaṇas.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Brahmayu, a native of the country of Mithilā.

He was advanced in years, being one hundred and twenty, and was profoundly versed in the various sūtras, the stars, and the arts of divination; he could foresee events before they had even sprouted, and was thus the preceptor of the entire nation.

Bramayu heard from afar that the Buddha, the son of a king and born of the Śākya clan, had left his country and its noble honors to become a śramaṇa; having attained the Way, he was titled Buddha, the Pure and Supreme One, who dwelt with five hundred śramaṇas in the kingdom of Sūrpāraka, transforming and enlightening sentient beings.
Bramayū reflected deeply and sighed in admiration: "The Śramaṇa Gautama is divine and majestic!

He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the one perfected in the supernormal powers of the Path, the Great Man, the Honored Hero, the Charioteer of Dharma, the Sage among sages, and the Teacher of gods and men. The defilements of his mind have been removed and all evils have been exhausted; having attained self-awakening, there is nothing he does not know. To śramaṇas, parivrājakas, Śakras, Brahmās, nāgas, and ghosts, he preaches the Dharma; his discourse—superior, intermediate, and inferior—is pure from the outset, profound, wondrous, and sublime, such as has never been heard by other sages."

Brahmayu explained this extensively to his disciples, saying, "He shall become the King of all Sages, the Unsurpassed, Truly Rightly Awakened One; we ought to prostrate ourselves before him and receive his transformative teachings."

Among the disciples of Shixin, there was one who was a "sublime sage" named Mōnà. He too was extensively learned in the scriptures, his clarity equaling that of his master. Having fully observed the secret prophecies, he knew that a Buddha was destined to appear; the physical marks of this being were extraordinary, numbering thirty-two, and his supreme dignity was peerless, penetrating the heart and illuminating all.
The Master said to the Māṇava:
"I have heard that Gautama is divine and unsurpassed, honored by all the devas; he speaks alone and walks solitary, yet is a hero among the holy ones. Go and behold him."
Is it not true that your venerable appearance and majestic bearing are truly grand models, as the many scholars have sighed in admiration?
If this is indeed so, I shall hasten to you to prostrate myself and pay my respects.
The Māṇavaka asked, "By what means should I observe this?
The Māṇava teacher replied:
"Does not the Sūtra say:

'In a future age there shall be a king named Śuddhodana and a queen named Māyā, whose bright virtue is perfectly complete. They shall give birth to a holy son, a God among Gods, whose uniquely exalted physical form measures sixteen feet in height and possesses the thirty-two marks. If he remains in the kingdom, he shall become a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin); if he renounces the kingdom for the Way and practices as a śramaṇa, he will certainly attain Buddhahood.'"

The Māṇava received the instruction, prostrated at his teacher’s feet, and went to the country of Sūrpāraka. He immediately approached the Buddha’s dwelling; after exchanging greetings, he withdrew and sat down with a tranquil mind.

He gazed intently at the marks and signs of the Buddha’s body, yet he did not perceive two characteristics: first, the broad and long tongue; second, the sheathed organ like that of a horse. His mind was filled with doubt.

Knowing that the Māṇava harbored doubts and expectations in his heart, the Buddha immediately manifested the sheathed organ through his supernormal power and extended his broad and long tongue to cover his face. He then touched both ears with it, withdrew the tongue back into his mouth, and emitted five-colored rays of light that circled his body three times before vanishing into the crown of his head.
Māṇava’s heart stirred with a mingling of joy and fear, and he sighed in delight, saying:
“The Śramaṇa Gautama is truly a Buddha!

His marks and signs and his radiance are fully perfected; such a sight is rare in the world. He may truly be called the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. I shall follow him to observe his noble model, so that I may transform my ignorance and delusion and also enlighten my teacher.”

He immediately sought out the World-Honored One’s location while dwelling in internal meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Wandering about to teach and transform others, he rescued and delivered sentient beings; whether staying overnight or returning home, he was always accompanied by the Saṃgha and never remained alone.
On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, as if a shadow follows the body, he beheld the majestic virtue of the divine transformations.
He bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet and took leave to return to his native land; upon arriving at his teacher’s place, he bowed as before and sat down in his seat.
The Master said:

"I shall send you to observe the qualities, the marks and signs, and the divine transformations of the Honored One Gautama; examine whether they truly accord with what the various scholars have praised without exaggeration."
"If it be so, I shall hasten to your presence to prostrate myself at your feet, offering the reverence of one who receives the dust from your feet upon his head.

He replied: "His physical marks and sublime virtue surpass those of heaven; he is so majestic as to be difficult to praise. Even Śakra and Brahmā cannot fathom him, and no multitude of sages can calculate his merit. He is the object of the praises of all the worthy, yet even after ten billion eons, not one part of his excellence has been attained. This is not something that my mere firefly-light of wisdom can fully describe."
To state the essentials briefly, there are thirty-two marks that transcend the world: first, the soles of the feet are level and even;
second, the hands and feet have wheels with a thousand spokes;
third, the bones are linked like hooks and chains.
The fourth mark is long fingers;
the fifth mark is full heels;
the sixth mark is hands and feet that are fine and soft, with palms and soles that are concave and convex respectively.
The seventh mark is that his hands and feet are joined with webs between the fingers and toes;
the eighth mark is that his calves are like those of an antelope;
the ninth mark is that his male organ is concealed within a sheath.
The tenth mark is that the body’s color is a radiant, shimmering purple-gold light;
the eleventh mark is that the body is like a diamond, with all flaws and impurities stilled;
the twelfth mark is that the skin is fine and soft, such that dust and water do not adhere to the body.
The thirteenth mark is that from each and every pore grows a single hair;
the fourteenth mark is that the hairs are deep blue-black in color, curling to the right;
the fifteenth mark is that the body is well-proportioned and square.
The sixteenth mark is that his upper body is like that of a lion;
the seventeenth mark is that his body is not crooked, being straight like the body of Brahmā;
the eighteenth mark is that his shoulders are full, with flesh well-developed and seamlessly attached to his torso.
Nineteenth, he stands upright with both hands reaching his knees;
twentieth, his jaw is like that of a lion;
twenty-first, he has forty teeth.
The twenty-second mark is that his teeth are even;
the twenty-third mark is that there are no gaps between his teeth;
the twenty-fourth mark is that his teeth are white beyond compare.
Twenty-fifth mark: A broad and long tongue;
twenty-sixth mark: A sense of taste that perceives every flavor in succession;
twenty-seventh mark: A voice like the sound of Brahmā.
The twenty-eighth mark: the seven parts are fully developed and prominent;
the twenty-ninth mark: the eyes are white with a deep blue-black tint;
the thirtieth mark: the eyelashes, both upper and lower, blink like those of a bull king.
The thirty-first mark is the white hair standing between his eyebrows;
the thirty-second mark is the fleshly protuberance upon his crown, its brilliant radiance eclipsing both sun and moon.

The śramaṇa Gautama possesses these noble and refined marks in their entirety, without a single deficiency. His divine and wondrous virtues are immeasurable; he is marvelous and precious, a rarity since antiquity.

“I observed that whenever Gautama took a step and raised his foot, he invariably lifted the right foot first; the length, shortness, and speed of his stride were perfectly harmonious with the proper ritual form.
When walking, his ankles and knees did not touch one another; he moved forward with his body level and his shoulders motionless.
If he wished to look back, he did so almost without effort, remaining poised for a moment before suddenly turning backward without twisting his torso.”
Neither bowing nor tilting his head, his body remained perfectly upright; he moved forward with a steady gaze, never looking back or to the side—such was the manner of his gait.
As Gautama traveled the road, the devas held up a precious canopy and flowers fell like snow;
neither devas, nāgas, nor birds dared to pass over him, and among all beings in the three realms, none could see the crown of his head.

The devas played music as they escorted and honored the Honored One; the nāgas, spirits, and terrestrial deities leveled the roads so that their elevations and depressions became as smooth as a whetstone.
His feet did not touch the ground, yet the marks of his wheels appeared as seals; his radiance shone with such brilliance that it did not fade for seven days.
The trees bent and rose up as if performing the ritual of kneeling and bowing.
When he goes to accept an invitation, he enters with his body level with the height of the lintel; if the lintel is not high, Gautama does not raise himself up.

He sits in the center of the couch without encroaching on the space before or behind it; sitting with hands joined, he never gestures or points, nor does he rest his chin upon his hand. When descending from the couch, he does not turn back, but descends suddenly to the ground.
When the celestial Māra approached with venomous intent, his mind felt no fear and his countenance became even more serene; through his compassionate pity for him, the venom was entirely dispelled.
He took water in his bowl, yet the bowl did not tilt or rise, and the water was neither too much nor too little;
when he washed the bowl, both the water and the bowl were utterly still, without the slightest sound.

He never placed his bowl on the ground; washing his hands within it, both his hands and the bowl were kept clean. When he removed the water from the bowl, whether moving it up or down, near or far, he always did so with perfect propriety.
He receives rice in his alms bowl without soiling it; when he takes a morsel of rice into his mouth, he chews it three times and then stops, so that no grain remains between his teeth.
He discerns each of the various flavors as they arise, yet this is sufficient to sustain his body, for he does not take pleasure in them.

Gautama accepts food for eight reasons: not for sport, without a mind of deviant conduct, without desire in his will, without artful hypocrisy, to distance himself from the dust of the three realms, to cause his will to dwell in the tranquility of the Way, to clothe himself in merit and attain deliverance, to sever old sensations and block the twelve seas, to extinguish past offenses and attain the power of the Way, and to maintain empty stillness without conceptualizing emptiness.
Wash the alms bowl as before.
Regarding the Dharma robes and the alms bowl, let the mind be free from both aversion and attachment.
Having finished reciting the sutras and offering prayers for the sake of the donors, return to the vihāra; do not speak to your disciples of the quality of the food you have eaten.
His food was digested spontaneously, and he was free from the impurities of excrement or urine.
Entering his chamber, he remained silent and deeply contemplated various meditative concentrations; he would emerge after a short while without ever missing the appointed time.
He neither slept nor dozed day or night.

He extensively expounded the clear Dharma to exhort his disciples, leading them into the Hall of the Way; he did not allow wealth or sensual desire to defile the conduct of the Way shown to his disciples.
His teachings were sublime and profound, beyond what could be heard or seen in the scriptures of immortals and sages; he inspired those dwelling with him to cultivate purity as the Way.

When walking in meditation, he did not look around or cast glances; his gait was neither hurried nor sluggish, and as he adjusted his robes, they fell gracefully over his body with a proper sense of tension and relaxation.
When entering the garden to wash his feet, he did not rub or wipe them, yet his feet were naturally clean.
The radiance of his body is as brilliant as celestial gold; his mind is unattached to craving, and his will is like empty space.

When he sits in meditative concentration, he is suddenly free from conceptualization. The three poisons, the four sufferings, the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the seven fetters, and the eight delusions—he extinguishes these delusions with unsurpassed illumination.

By means of the concentrations of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, one severs the nine abodes of the gods; by means of the ten wholesome deeds, one eliminates the ten unwholesome deeds; one composes the twelve divisions of the scriptures and uproots the twelve links of dependent origination. Thus, the afflictions and sores of the sixty-two views, as well as the turbid thoughts of the mind, become utterly tranquil.

Having already delivered his own venerable body through the four immeasurables and the Mahāyāna, he further seeks to save all sentient beings; yet, wishing to proclaim the sublime model, the disciple had not yet questioned him when [the Buddha] first smiled, and from his mouth issued forth a radiance that circled his body three times before gradually fading away.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated himself, and questioned him; the Buddha then expounded the Dharma extensively, his voice possessing eight qualities:

the most excellent sound, the easily understood sound, the soft and gentle sound, the harmonious and well-modulated sound, the sound of noble wisdom, the unerring sound, the profound and wondrous sound, and the non-feminine sound.
His speech was never faltering or deficient, and no one could find any flaw in it.

Whenever he preached the great sutras, the gods of the twenty-four heavens, Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings, as well as the sun, moon, and stars—the deities, kings, ministers, and subjects therein, along with the terrestrial spirits and sea dragons—all came to prostrate themselves and listen to the sutra individually. As the sound of the sutra entered their ears, each understood it in their own respective language.

The Buddha’s luminous wisdom is like the River of Kunlun; thousands of streams and ten thousand currents all look up to it, yet though the rivers overflow and fill, the river itself does not diminish by so much as a single drop.
The Buddha’s illumination surpasses all others; sentient beings receive wisdom and each attains fulfillment, yet the Buddha’s illumination does not diminish by so much as a hair’s breadth.

When the discourse on the sutra was concluded, the honored bodhisattvas, the celestial kings, the sovereigns, subjects, dragons, and spirits were all filled with joy; they prostrated themselves and withdrew, reverently upholding and practicing its teachings.
He entered the inner quarters in profound silence, never treating his disciples or even sentient beings with contempt despite the supreme virtue of the World-Honored One.

"I followed Gautama for six months, as a shadow follows the body, observing in full detail his daily activities: rising and resting, walking meditation, entering the room, washing and rinsing, eating and drinking, offering prayers, preaching the sutras, and exhorting his disciples during their periods of meditative concentration."

The Māṇava said: “Gautama, your majestic appearance and dignified demeanor are such that what I have described is like adding a single drop to the great ocean; it cannot be grasped by the thoughts of the multitude of sages, nor can it be fully reached by the gods, nor can it be discussed by heaven and earth. Sublime indeed and unsurpassed, vast indeed and boundless, it is beyond measurement and calculation, and difficult to describe in its entirety.”
Having heard of the Virtue of the Celestial Master from his disciples, Brahmayu was struck with astonishment and wept, saying:
"My years are now at their end; I have nearly lived my life in vain and died in vain, for I did not behold the supreme brilliance of the Celestial Master."
Moyu said joyfully, "I have met with fortune!
To die beholding the Buddha— its glory is beyond words."
"Though a fool may possess a lifespan as long as heaven and earth, how is he any different from the class of soil and stone?
He then immediately adjusted his robes, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and bowed his head three times, saying:
"I take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Sangha."
"I pray that my remaining life may be prolonged, so that I may have the opportunity to behold you, prostrate myself before you, and receive your transformative teachings.
With the clarity of his six supernormal powers, the Buddha perceived her seeking refuge; he accepted her from afar.
From the kingdom of Sotthivati, he arrived at the kingdom of Mithilā and sat beneath a tree.
The king, his ministers, the people, and the householders of the Śākya clan took turns exhorting one another, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."

Born as the son of a sovereign from the lineage of the Śākya kings, he ought to have lived in luxury and splendor; yet now his character is pure and simple, his aspirations are tranquil and detached. He is free from the stain of greed and lust, the poison of anger and resentment, and the darkness of ignorance. Standing above all sages, he is like the moon among the stars. His divine virtue extends widely, and he is venerated by all the heavens. He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; the defilements and darkness are utterly exhausted, while the light of wisdom alone remains. His spiritual sanctity is abundant and complete. Regarding the myriad phenomena within heaven and earth, he clearly perceives their present manifestations throughout the ten directions in all their minute details; as for future events that have not yet sprouted, there is nothing he does not understand. When he utters his teachings and bestows his instructions, every word is true and sincere.
The king, his ministers, and the high-minded sages all said in unison:

"It is a fortunate time for us to have been born to behold the Celestial Teacher, one who is worthy of honor and veneration; we should prostrate ourselves before him and bathe in his divine transformation."
Consequently, they gathered together; among those in carriages, on horses, or on foot, not a single person remained at home.
Upon their arrival, some bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet, some knelt, some exchanged formal salutations, and some introduced themselves by name; all then sat down in silence.

When Brahmāyu heard that the Buddha had arrived together with his assembly of noble disciples, he was filled with immeasurable joy. He led his own disciples and went together to the place where the Buddha was.
Just as he reached the edge of the grove, a thought occurred to him:
"Should I not first dispatch someone to express my heart’s devotion? Would it be disrespectful to proceed directly myself?"
He called to his disciple, saying:
"Take my name and prostrate yourself at the feet of the Buddha, saying:

'Brahmayu has reached the age of one hundred and twenty; he hungers for the Sage’s model and delights in admiring his pure wind. He rejoices that Gautama’s daily life is ever peaceful, tranquil, and free from desire.'"

"I have now come to request an audience. The disciple prostrated to his teacher and immediately went to the Buddha's location. Having performed his head-prostrations, he fully recounted his teacher’s request and addressed the Buddha in praise of his master, saying:

"The National Preceptor Brahmayu is profoundly versed in all the scriptures and has mastered the secret prophecies. He dwells in quietude within his chamber of purification and foreknows the celestial phenomena; there is no auspicious or inauspicious sign in the charts and books that he does not foresee. He has long known that this world shall have a Celestial Teacher—one of colossal stature, sixteen feet tall, with a natural countenance like purple gold, possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, the God among Gods and King among all Sages."

"I have now hurried here to take refuge in the Three Honored Ones; staying just outside the forest trees, I did not dare advance further. I wish to have an audience and reverently receive your divine instruction.
The World-Honored One then said, "Excellent! Come forward!"
The disciple returned and reported to his master, fully explaining the Buddha’s clear instructions; the master immediately prostrated himself on the ground and approached with joyful delight.
At that time, the householder Śreṇika of the country, seeing his master from afar, was struck with awe and trembling; with hands folded and head bowed, he said:
"Return to your usual seat; I shall now sit by the side of Gautama, the World-Honored One, who is the charioteer of the Dharma."
He immediately prostrated himself, touching his five limbs to the ground, and bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet; then he sat with reverent composure.

With a tranquil mind and clear heart, he gazed intently at the features of the Buddha’s body. He saw thirty of the Buddha’s wondrous marks, yet two marks did not appear. Confused and harboring doubt, he bowed his head to the ground and asked in verse:
“In my Brahmin scriptures, The secret prophecies record the essentials of the world;”
In this turbid age, the king was named Śuddhodana, and the queen was named Māyā;
the crown prince was named Siddhārtha, his countenance radiant with the luster of purple-gold,
his body endowed with the marks of a World-Honored One, who governed by means of the Dharma while enduring impurities.
Does he possess the marks of the supreme and true appearance, the thirty-two in their entirety?
Is his private organ retracted in pure chastity, such that it cannot be distinguished as having desire?
Does he indeed have a broad and long tongue, capable of covering his face and reaching his ears?
Do your methods of teaching surpass those of all other sages? Is this not something rarely heard even by Brahmā and Śakra?
As a clear guide and teacher of gods and men, are you able to utterly dispel the doubts of the multitude?
Embracing the Way while dwelling in the world in peace, will you attain the state of an immortal in a future life?
"Does the Immortal dwell in Nirvana, forever departing from the three realms?
Can the mind, consciousness, intellect, and soul extinguish all suffering? The Brahmin set forth the doubts in his heart.

The Buddha, fully knowing the two aspects of the Brahmin’s doubt, immediately manifested the "horse-organ hidden in the sheath" (*aśvakośa*) through his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). He extended his broad and long tongue until it covered his face and reached his left and right ears. The radiance from his mouth illuminated the country of Mithilā, circled his body three times, and slowly returned into his mouth. He then addressed him, saying:
"As for what you have asked regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Being: I am fully endowed with these marks, lacking not even one.

Since incalculable kalpas past, I have practiced the four immeasurable minds and cultivated generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. I have rescued and delivered sentient beings as I would protect my own body; I have severed all seeking, contemplated emptiness, and maintained the state of non-conceptual absorption. The defilements of my mind have been entirely eliminated, leaving not even a trace of obscuration. Through the accumulation of these practices, all calamities have been extinguished; through the gathering of myriad virtues, I have attained the Buddha-body. With its marks and signs and radiant light, I walk alone in the three realms, forever departing from the ignorance and darkness of the five paths of existence, and having obtained the brilliance of the Unsurpassed Honored One—therefore, I am called a Buddha."

If there remains within the mind even a hair’s breadth of the poison of lust, anger, and ignorance, or the darkness of the five aggregates and six sense-fields, the Way of the Buddha will not be accomplished.

If there were anyone who, from the past until the present, regarding the thoughts of sentient beings, or throughout the countless kalpas yet to come, had not fully understood all their intricate and profound matters, that person would not be a Buddha.

The four fearlessnesses, the eight voices, the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics—if even one of these is lacking, one is not a Buddha.
I am now fully endowed with all things and lack nothing; therefore, I am called a Buddha.

A śramaṇa who has attained the Way of Arhatship can divide one body into ten, ten into a hundred, a hundred into a thousand, a thousand into ten thousand, and ten thousand into countless bodies; he can also merge countless bodies back into a single one.

By pressing the earth with his finger, he causes the trichiliocosm to tremble; this is because he has attained the concentration of desirelessness through his mental cultivation, so how much more so for a Buddha!

The virtue of a single mark upon the Buddha’s brow could be counted as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the merit of the space between his brows is difficult even to calculate—how much more so the virtue of his entire body!

He spoke again: "Brahmin, those who place their faith in the Three Honored Ones of the Buddha will enjoy peace and security in this life and be reborn in the heavens after death. Whatever you desire shall be granted according to your thoughts; whatever you doubt, you should ask, for do not hesitate to inquire."
The brahmin thought to himself:
"What Gautama has spoken is profound, subtle, and far-reaching; it exhausts all my questions.
He then thought again:
"Should I now inquire about matters of the present life,
or matters of future lives? Thinking thus,
he again attained awakening and said:
"The essentials of the three periods of time are illuminated only by the Buddha; how could they possibly be perceived by immortals, sages, or the various Confucian scholars?
The Brahmin asked, "What is meant by 'one whose mind has departed' (śramaṇa)?"
What is meant by "thorough penetration"?
What is meant by "purity"?
What is meant by "tranquility"?
"What do you mean by 'Buddha'?
The Buddha replied to the brahmin:
"I shall explain this with true words to clarify your understanding; listen attentively and take it to heart."
To attain the three bases of supernormal power is called the "mind that has gone beyond.

To clearly discern the past and distinguish the places of birth, seeing with the eye of the Way such that neither mountain nor stone can obstruct one, dispelling darkness and resolving doubts so that the three periods of time are all clearly illuminated—this is called "penetrating mastery."
Having attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and with the defilements of the mind eradicated, this is called "tranquility" (*śānti*).
With the three poisons (*triviṣa*) extinguished and the mind like celestial gold, this is called "purity" (*viśuddhi*).

When the root of ignorance regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is incinerated without remainder, and the practice of the pure path descends upon the triple world (*traidhātuka*), such that all delusions are exhausted and no longer reach the infinite, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); thus, the honored title "Buddha" is bestowed.

The brahmin rose joyfully and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, placing his head and face at the Buddha’s feet. He kissed the Buddha’s feet with his mouth and rubbed them with his hands, then addressed him by name:
“I am the brahmin Vāmamara Śreṣṭhin; I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṃgha.”
Shedding tears, he said:

"Sentient beings are shrouded in darkness, obscured by the six obscurations; they behold the Buddha but do not revere him, see the sutras but do not read them, and encounter śramaṇas yet harbor no heart of piety or love. They do not receive his divine transformation—this is indeed a cause for long-term decline!"
Seeing their teacher’s complete devotion, his disciples looked at one another and said, "Our venerable teacher is profoundly versed in the scriptures;

there is no book he has not read. His fame spreads throughout the four quarters, and he is honored by all scholars. Yet now he humbles himself, joining his palms and bowing his head at the feet of Gautama—how much more so should we!"
The Buddha said to the brahmin: "Sit again.
I clearly perceive your mind; you possess true faith and wisdom directed toward the World-Honored One."

Having received these instructions, they took their seats. The Buddha again spoke of the virtue of observing the precepts, the merit of giving, and the removal of the defilements of household impurity, extolling the superior practice of those whose resolve is set upon the Way.
The Buddha immediately perceived that the brahmin possessed the mind of a superior person—one of joy and broad understanding—and for his sake, he expounded the essentials of the supreme path:

"All myriad forms of suffering arise from the body; the wise man, through deep illumination, knows that what is called 'pleasure' is but a delusion. By reversing the flow of existence and seeking its source, one reaches primordial non-being (*anādikāla*); this is called the wisdom and clarity of the superior person regarding the true reality."
One does not realize that the body’s most grievous sufferings all arise from habitual conditioning;
when the superior person awakens to this, such clarity constitutes the ultimate truth.
The three realms are like an illusion: where there is union, there must be separation; how can anything flourish without decaying?

When causes and conditions combine, calamity arises; when all conditions disperse, suffering ceases. The superior person contemplates the root and thereby knows its emptiness; this clarity is the True Dharma.

By knowing that the root is non-existent, one attains mastery over the triple world. Emptying the mind and purifying conduct, one does not crave various desires and attains the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). When what is grasped by the mind is thus transformed, the Three Honored Ones can be attained.
The brahmin’s mind was liberated, like fine white cotton cloth—pure and free from defilement—that takes on color when placed in dye.

Thus it was with the brahmin’s mind: having repeatedly served various Buddhas in past lives and practiced pure precepts, now hearing the Honored One’s teaching, he fully understood the path of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment. The impurities of his mind were stilled and exhausted; he entered the three gates of liberation and was forever separated from all suffering.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Before I had seen the Buddha, I harbored great errors in my conduct; obscured by blindness and darkness, I believed the words of mad and foolish men to be the ultimate truth."

Now that I have finally beheld the Buddha, my madness has been healed; the blind see, the deaf hear, the mute speak, and the hunchbacked straighten themselves; those imprisoned in the jail have been released.

How tragic it is that commoners, deluded and ignorant, lead lives in vain and die in vain, failing to embrace the flavor of the Tathāgata’s true Way, and remaining forever in the agony of the flaming fires! What can be done?
What a fortunate birth of mine!
To have encountered the Buddha’s supreme spiritual power and had him personally explain to me the most profound Way, enabling me to return to my original state and abide eternally in non-action.

From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Bhikṣus. I vow to be a lay follower of pure faith, upholding benevolence by not killing, practicing contentment by not stealing, maintaining chastity by not committing adultery, holding fast to faith by not deceiving, and fulfilling filial piety by not drinking intoxicants.
"The World-Honored One has taken pity on me; I pray that tomorrow at dawn, together with the assembly of sages, you will deign to accept my humble meal.
The Buddha silently accepted his invitation.
The Brahmin, his heart filled with joy, prostrated at the Buddha's feet and returned home to prepare a meal of a hundred flavors.
At dawn, he performed prostrations before the Buddha within his own home and knelt upright, respectfully declaring:
"I pray that the Buddha will deign to grace us with your presence at this time.
The Buddha, having properly donned his dharma robes, arrived at the brahmin’s house together with the assembly of noble disciples, and they all took their places upon the Dharma seats.
The brahmin personally performed the ritual ablutions and made offerings with a reverent mind for seven days in this manner.
When the Buddha had finished expounding his divine transformations, he returned to the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
Before long, the brahmin passed away.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they went together to inform the Buddha:
"Now that the brahmin has died, by what path will his mind be directed?"
The World-Honored One said:

"That brahmin possessed a noble mind of broad understanding that had reached the stage of non-returning; his five hindrances were exhausted and purified like celestial gold. Having attained purity therein, he departed as an arhat into the unconditioned."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus rejoiced.
*The Brahmāyu Sūtra*.
